source.title: Probing the Limits of Compressive Memory: A Study of Infini-Attention in Small-Scale Pretraining
source.authors: Rui-Zhe Huang; Kexuan Zhang; Yihao Fang; Baifeng Yu

record.file_problem: The abstract begins with a clipped fragment (“ployable computational efficiencies”); the remainder of the paper, including its main sections and appendices, is present.
record.tranche_reason: Compares training loss for a baseline and an alternative attention architecture at the same stated parameter count. This bears conceptually on architectural sensitivity, but it does not fit or test scaling laws.
record.gate_note: The paper reports one 300M-parameter model pair, not sweeps over parameter count, tokens, or compute, and reports training rather than held-out loss. It does not test power-law fits, extrapolation, compute-optimal allocation, or downstream predictability with scale. Benchmark scores and retrieval results are not rows because they do not measure a claim version’s scaling relationship.
record.test_reason: The paper cites Kaplan et al. only as motivation. It trains one 300M-parameter LLaMA pair (baseline vs Infini-attention) for ~983M tokens and fits no scaling relationship. The loss comparison does not test V4. Infini-attention is a memory-augmented attention mechanism, not a depth/width/shape variation. Its memory was rarely exercised because nearly all sequences fit in one segment. The two runs also used different learning rates (6e-5 vs 1.2e-4). The measure is training loss, not held-out loss.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors conclude that Infini-attention trains effectively and stably at 300M scale, avoiding the baseline's vanishing gradients. It reaches comparable training loss and improves long-context retrieval (up to 31% over baseline). Its benefit is limited by the short training sequences and by degradation from repeated memory compression. They make no scaling-law claim.
record.recipe_differences: The original sources study loss scaling across model, data, and compute scales; this paper compares two attention configurations at one model size and reports training loss.
record.method_sensitivity: The baseline required a higher learning rate (1.2 × 10−4) for stable training; the Infini-attention model used 6 × 10−5.

fits_no_version.finding: At 300M parameters and ~983M FineWeb tokens, Infini-attention and a standard-attention baseline reach similar final training loss (~3.72 vs 3.68). The baseline needed a doubled learning rate.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Swapping in compressive-memory attention at a fixed small model size changes pretraining loss little when training sequences are short.

record.problems: Only one model size and one baseline/alternative architecture comparison are used for the relevant result. The reported loss is training loss, not held-out loss; no uncertainty is stated for the loss values. The text notes substantial fluctuations in both loss curves.
record.rows_left_out: No other rows bear on the tested scaling-law versions. Retrieval and benchmark results do not measure a version’s scaling relationship.

untested.parts: No sweep over parameters, tokens or compute.
No depth/width/shape variation at fixed parameter count. Only one attention-mechanism swap, at one size.
No other modality or regime scaling.
Benchmarks are reported at a single scale, not related to scale or loss.
No exponents or fitting choices are compared.

record.verdict_notes: The reader's V4 'supports' label is removed. The comparison is not a shape-at-fixed-size test, it uses one size only, and it is confounded by learning rate. The memory mechanism was largely inactive, so near-equal loss says little about architecture sensitivity.

versions.untested_parts: No held-out-loss scaling sweep over parameters, tokens, or compute.
No small-run fits or predictions of larger runs.
No fixed-compute allocation sweep or parameter/token growth trend.
Only one attention-mechanism comparison at 300M parameters is reported; depth, width, and a wide range of architecture settings are not varied.
No other modality or training-regime scaling-law tests.
Downstream benchmarks are reported, but not as a relationship to model scale or pretraining loss.
No comparison of fitting choices or exponents, and no analysis of bending scaling curves.

rows.subject: Infini-attention model
rows.operation_detail: Pretrained with Infini-attention; reports training-loss trajectory and final loss.
rows.note: The text says the models converge to comparable asymptotic performance and neither consistently outperforms the other over the loss trajectory; both curves fluctuate. This is training loss, not held-out loss.
rows.check: This is a single-size training-loss comparison of an attention-mechanism swap, not a shape variation at fixed parameter count. The memory path was barely used, since 'nearly all training sequences fall within just one segment'. The run is confounded by a different learning rate from the baseline. The final loss (~3.72) is read from text or figure, with no uncertainty.

rows.subject: baseline model
rows.operation_detail: Pretrained with memory disabled; reports training-loss trajectory and final loss.
rows.note: The text says the models converge to comparable asymptotic performance and neither consistently outperforms the other over the loss trajectory; both curves fluctuate. Baseline learning rate was raised to 1.2 × 10−4 for stable training. This is training loss, not held-out loss.
rows.check: Comparator to r1, with the same issues. Its learning rate was doubled to 1.2e-4 to avoid vanishing gradients, so architecture is confounded with optimisation settings. The measure is training loss, not held-out loss.

source_check.scope: Only the listed rows, labels and statements were checked; presence is not whole-study approval.

reader_labels.label: supports
reader_labels.condition: The tested 300M-parameter baseline and Infini-attention models under the reported pretraining setup
reader_labels.reason: Their final training losses are close and the authors describe their asymptotic performance and overall loss trajectories as comparable (r1–r2). This is evidence for this single architecture comparison, not a wide-range architecture sweep.
